title: The lions' den (Daniel 6)
hookLine: Daniel prays at his window three times a day, law or no law

cards: The lions' den often gets told as a young hero's story. Follow the book's own timeline instead. Daniel was carried off to Babylon as a youth.
Now Babylon itself has fallen, and a new ruler, Darius, sits on the throne. Daniel has outlasted the kings who took him.
After a lifetime in government, he's so honest and capable that Darius plans to set him over the whole kingdom. The other officials can't stand it. They hunt for corruption and find none.
Finally they say: we'll never catch him, unless it's about the law of his God.

teach.h: A DECREE: PRAY ONLY TO THE KING.
teach.b: So they flatter the king: make a decree that for thirty days, no one may pray to any god or person except you. Break it, and you go to the lions. Darius signs, and by the law of the Medes and Persians it can't be changed.

In the King James Bible: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime."
As he did aforetime. No protest. No closed shutters either.
He just keeps doing what he's always done, at a window facing a city he hasn't seen since he was young. The habit was already there; the law simply found it.

Three times a day echoes a psalm: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." Jewish tradition keeps three daily times of prayer, and synagogues traditionally face toward Jerusalem. The officials catch him.
The king, who has set his heart on saving Daniel, tries until sundown and can't. Daniel goes in, and a stone seals the den. The king spends the night fasting and sleepless.
At dawn he calls into the den: is thy God able to deliver thee from the lions?
And from inside: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me."
Christian readers often hear this as a call to steady, daily faithfulness, ready before the test comes.

how: Some Christians keep fixed times of daily prayer, morning, midday and evening, through the Liturgy of the Hours, the Angelus, the Book of Common Prayer offices or simple personal habit; Jewish tradition prays three daily services, facing Jerusalem.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: pray only to the king, thirty days
the king runs to the den

s: Daniel was a young man when he was thrown to the lions
by the book's timeline he was taken as a youth and has outlasted Babylon's kings.
Daniel kept praying just as he had before the decree
"as he did aforetime": three times a day, at the open window.
Daniel closed his shutters to pray in secret
his windows were open toward Jerusalem.

games.q: you've heard the decree is signed: anyone who prays to God for thirty days goes to the lions. it's time for your usual prayer. what do you do?
o: skip it for thirty days; God understands.
pray in secret, with the windows shut.
pray as always, at the open window.
games.why: "he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." no protest, no hiding. just the habit.

practice: Choose three moments in your day to pause, even for thirty seconds, after breakfast, at lunch, before sleep: three windows to turn your face toward. Then take the first pause now: be still, breathe, and give thanks for one thing.
If you pray, pray as Daniel did, with thanks; if not, simply stop and notice.

wordCard.voice: Darius. The king who signed the decree that trapped Daniel, then spent a sleepless night trying to save the man he'd set over his kingdom.

orig.note: Aramaic: the den of lions. this chapter of Daniel is written in Aramaic.
